name: Dasiglucagon
evidenceNote: Dasiglucagon was approved in 2021 on the strength of three randomized, placebo-controlled trials in adults and children with type 1 diabetes. FDA widened the pediatric label in 2026.
summary: Dasiglucagon (Zegalogue) is a ready-to-inject glucagon analog approved in 2021 for severe low blood sugar in people with diabetes.
keyTakeaway: Dasiglucagon is a modified form of glucagon, the hormone that tells the liver to release sugar. Unlike older glucagon kits that must be mixed before use, it is stable as a ready-to-inject liquid. In its main adult trial, half of treated patients had recovered within 10 minutes; on placebo that took 40. FDA approved it as Zegalogue in 2021 for severe hypoglycemia in diabetes, and in 2026 extended it to children weighing at least 20 kg. FDA's database now lists both Zegalogue presentations as discontinued. It is not approved for congenital hyperinsulinism.

blocks.text: Dasiglucagon is a glucagon analog: a 29-amino-acid peptide built to act like glucagon, the hormone that raises blood sugar [1]. It is used as a rescue medicine for severe hypoglycemia, a dangerous drop in blood sugar that can cause confusion, seizures or loss of consciousness, most often in people who use insulin.

Natural glucagon is unstable in liquid, so traditional emergency kits ship it as a powder that a caregiver must mix with water during the emergency. Dasiglucagon was designed to stay stable in an aqueous (water-based) solution, so it comes ready to inject [2]. It was sold as Zegalogue in a single-dose autoinjector and a prefilled syringe [1].

The liver stores sugar as glycogen, a chain of glucose molecules. Dasiglucagon binds glucagon receptors on liver cells, which triggers the breakdown of glycogen and the release of glucose into the bloodstream [1].

That mechanism has a built-in limit: it only works if the liver has glycogen to give. People who are starving, have adrenal insufficiency (underactive adrenal glands), or have had low blood sugar for a long time may not respond, and need glucose instead [1]. After injection under the skin, the drug reaches its highest level in about 35 minutes and has a half-life of about 30 minutes, and in adults blood sugar rose by an average of 168 mg/dL within 90 minutes [1].

Yes. FDA approved dasiglucagon as Zegalogue on March 22, 2021, as a new molecular entity. In June 2026, FDA approved a supplement that redefined the pediatric population by body weight rather than age, so the label now covers any adult with diabetes and any child with diabetes whose body weight is 20 kg or more [1][3].

Approval and availability are separate questions. As of late 2026, FDA's Drugs@FDA database lists the marketing status of both the autoinjector and the prefilled syringe as discontinued, even though the approval itself remains in place [3]. People who rely on a glucagon rescue product can confirm with a pharmacist which options are currently stocked.

blocks.text: Dasiglucagon has a single approved use, as emergency treatment for severe low blood sugar in people with diabetes, covering adults and children of 20 kg or more. Its safety and effectiveness have not been established in children below that weight [1]. The label directs anyone giving it to call for emergency help right after the injection and, once the person responds, to give sugar by mouth [1].

Approval rested on three randomized, double-blind trials in type 1 diabetes, in which hypoglycemia was induced with insulin under medical supervision. The main measure was time until blood sugar rose by at least 20 mg/dL without rescue glucose [1][2].

blocks.text: Dasiglucagon has also been studied as a continuous infusion in children with congenital hyperinsulinism, a rare condition in which the pancreas releases too much insulin. A phase 3 trial in 32 children was completed in 2020 [4]. That use is not part of the approved label [1].

Stomach upset is the main side effect. In the two placebo-controlled adult trials, nausea occurred in 57% of people given dasiglucagon versus 4% on placebo, and vomiting in 25% versus 2%. Headache, diarrhea and pain at the injection site were less common. Children reported nausea, vomiting, headache and injection site pain [1].

The label lists two conditions in which it should not be used. In pheochromocytoma, a tumor of the adrenal gland, it can trigger a sharp rise in blood pressure. In insulinoma, an insulin-secreting tumor, it can raise blood sugar briefly and then provoke a rebound drop. Allergic reactions, including rare anaphylaxis, have been reported with glucagon products [1].

It can interact with other medicines. People taking beta-blockers may have a short-lived rise in pulse and blood pressure. Indomethacin can blunt its effect on blood sugar, and dasiglucagon may strengthen the blood-thinning effect of warfarin [1].
